b: I told my father I was moving out of his house the day it happened. It was ammi’s idea to tell him at the very last minute – that way, his anger would last only as long as the movers took to load their Suzuki with my stuff. With bloodshot eyes, my father watched me drive away – to another part of the city, where my childhood best friend Aesha and I had found an apartment for ourselves.

Salute to the girls who do this here, in Karachi: live outside of blood, family, marriage or whatever patriarchal bargain most women in my city use to seek their freedom. Anam was the first girl I saw who did this – who did not transfer, like property, from her father’s house to a husband’s, but instead lived with two others in this sprawling city of at least 20 million, but very likely more, home to every ethnic and religious group in Pakistan. Its indigenous communities were historically fisherfolk, pastoralists, and Sindhi and Baloch people, but modern Karachi was founded and funded by Sindhi Hindus and Parsis and Gujaratis. Post-partition, it became home to Muhajirs, who migrated from India, as well as millions of Pashtuns from northern Pakistan and Afghanistan. In the city’s mix are also migrants from Punjab and Balochistan, Burma and Bangladesh. Every kind of population has laid its stake to the city, so why not single women?
The author in her street. Photo by Aesha

We might be one of the tiniest populations in Karachi’s history to fight for our right to the city. A friend from Bangalore visited and, after we’d walked the old streets of Kharadar and the shiny roads of Clifton, she said, baffled: ‘And I thought we in India had few women on the streets.’ Where were the akeli women? She meant unaccompanied women – not the rich-girl variety who outsource their lives to drivers and guards who shuttle them around the city in protective containers, but middle-class girls like us.

‘My family lives in another city,’ I’d told my landlord, nervously avoiding his gaze. In Karachi, respectable girls did this only under the pretext of majboori – some justifiable excuse grounded in necessity, like working or studying away from home. Otherwise, only sex workers and trans women typically broke away from their families to live an unconventional life, one far more difficult than mine. Turned out he hardly cared. The apartment was cheap and, given the neighbourhood it was in – Badar Commercial, an unruly stretch in an otherwise upscale residential part of town, where the lane was not well kept and the building did not have a lock – he wasn’t looking for respectability points. Most others, landlords and landladies alike, had looked at me and said: ‘Families only.’ They did not want to hand over their apartment to two girls, all akeli, all alone, by themselves. Potential blemishes. Danger.

When we moved into the building at Badar, we anticipated all kinds of eyes. The apartment opposite ours was a lawyer’s office, or posed as one. Upstairs lived a gruff old uncle, a retired policeman who fought with everyone and threatened to call the cops after arguments. All day, he slept with the rooftop keys, effectively controlling access to the building’s water tanks.

The two apartments below us belonged to a family that had bought both units and broken down the middle wall. There were lots of women and children and a little dog. The ‘man of the house’ was a 21-year-old boy, evidently a drug addict who was usually found by the entrance staircase, getting high and holding a gun. His 20-year-old wife, a decade younger than us, was friendly. She asked us how we managed, all akelay. Again that word. We got into the habit of saying: ‘Yes, God knows how we manage, all akelay, all saath saath.’ Alone-together.
Since she’d been over a few times, we told her that the gun made us feel queasy. Could her husband please put it away? Very calmly, she replied: ‘He has never pointed it at you, has he?’
The neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely

Our balcony faced the balcony of the building opposite ours. The grilles were close enough to talk to the person on the other side. We knew these neighbours only at this elevation: it was the COVID-19 pandemic era, so everyone was stuck inside. WhatsApp numbers were exchanged; regretted it instantly. Uncle A had an on-again, off-again relationship with his wife, which meant he sometimes rang me up in the middle of the night, sobbing. Aunty B, wonderful to chat with during the day, was obsessed with jinns at night. She loved sending us links to YouTube videos where such supernatural beings were summoned into a courtroom, and she wanted to know if we, too, had ever seen one.

Badar Commercial – with its cast of characters all breaking the codes of Pakistani respectability in some way – got used to us faster than we got used to it. But the neighbourhood did wonder about us. We had friends over a lot, and family rarely. We sometimes dressed respectably – shalwar kameez and saris – whereas other times I walked around Badar in knee-length shorts and tank tops. We spoke English but also Urdu, Kutchi and Memoni; one of us was a teacher and the other a psychologist, but was that really all we did? And were we really Muslim? Often, at home, or grocery shopping, or having chai at the streetside dhaba, or tea-shop, someone would ask: Hindu? Christian? Foreign?

This inability to categorise us reached its pinnacle after a Qawwali night at our apartment – a Sufi music performance. A neighbour who had invited himself midway through the performance after hearing it from his window later asked us with utter confusion: ‘Are you Sunni or Shia?’
He leaned in uncomfortably close and whispered: ‘You are the Illuminati?’

Some men assumed we were sex workers and showed up at our door. This might have been my father’s deepest fear: if my family discovered I lived akelay, they’d think me a loose woman, and him a dishonourable man who could not keep his property in line. My extended family continued to believe I still lived with my parents. If an uncle visited, he was told I was out of town. ‘Sadia goes to Hyderabad a lot,’ my relatives noted.

Our time in that apartment was spent, really, undoing our lives. Aesha and I came from families where a room of your own was a luxury only richer relatives afforded their children. Until I was 16, I shared a room with my parents and four siblings; after that, there were two rooms, one for my parents and one for us. Now, Aesha and I each had a room, with a door we could close behind us and let nothing in for a while. At first, I did not know what to do with the emptiness. Just me and my friend, and a feeling of being untethered, unpropertied. We wanted others to feel it too, so our home was always filled with friends and women and anyone who needed a place to crash.

We set up the space with what little we had. Our mothers donated precious items from their kitchens. (When she came over, I introduced ammi to the neighbourhood women – trying to prove, I think, that it was possible to not live a double life, to have both my freedom and my mother by my side.) Our friends gave us our first furniture: a floor rug, a cupboard. We raised and killed too many plants, and washed our clothes by hand or sent them home when the water was out again. We learned to interact with the city in ways we never had before: comparing the vegetable vendors’ rates and learning who had been taking advantage of us, becoming experts at shortcuts on foot, especially during the rain, and knowing where to find rickshaws at 6 pm versus 9 pm.
For the first time, I prayed under the open sky while the city raged around me

Karachi is a logistical nightmare for anyone who lives here – and none of its systems are designed to include women in their public unfolding. Every bank vendor and dhaba server and home electrician is a man. This was another city that opened up to us: of everyday upkeep and haggling and bills. In this city, we learned to be less afraid of the men we had been taught to be suspicious of our whole lives: the electrician boys, the plumber uncles, the carpenter brothers. While any kind of man can turn uncomfortably friendly at a moment’s notice, there’s a way both patriarchy and capitalism benefit by insisting that the working-class man is the biggest threat to a woman’s safety. Under this ruse, the ‘good’ men in my life can surveil and control my movements, while a whole world of centrally airconditioned, securitised and gatekept enterprises can capitalise on this idea of keeping out the riff-raff.

In Badar Commercial, this lie came further undone. Plumber #1 was younger than us, fascinated by our women-only lives, and before leaving would help himself to swigs of whatever alcohol we had left over. Electrician uncle was popular among all the single girlies and slowly taught us how to drill the walls and reinstall ceiling fans. Plumber #2 was of a more conservative bent, refusing to look us straight in the eye but kindly and non-patronisingly telling us we had burned, nay destroyed, our new water heater.

At the roadside dhabas where I read books and people-watched, I often met men not from my world. M J, a rickshaw-wallah, learned my daily routines and routes, and knew exactly which friend lived where, and where I went and what I bought. I, in turn, learned about his life, one among thousands of Pashtuns who migrate from the northwest to seek a better life here. He had two jobs, sent money home to a family he maybe saw once a year, yet made less than our monthly rent. M J was beloved by everyone he met, punctual to a fault, and smoked two packs a day. He said: ‘Sadi, if you weren’t a girl, I’d invite you to Ludo nights with the boys.’ We went everywhere in his grand rickshaw that he’d decorated himself, every inch of it shiny and tasselled. I loved sitting amid all those colours. For the first time, with him, I prayed under the open sky in Karachi, touched the grass with my forehead while the city raged around me. We were by the sea; he rolled out his janamaz to pray and offered that yes, I could do it too if I wanted, why not?

I think we got away with living in that apartment because it was in a seedy neighbourhood where everyone knew everyone’s shit but collectively agreed not to meddle unless things got really out of hand. In close quarters, noise is not contained. Everyone knew when Uncle A and his wife were fighting, or whose side Aunty B took when her sons clashed over the eaten biryani. And when the retired officer upstairs sent cops after the drug-boy on the first floor, the whole neighbourhood knew, because men with guns were banging on our doors at 3 am.

There were conflicting accounts. One neighbour said the boy downstairs sold ice, others said he consumed it, yes, but did not sell. Everyone agreed he was high out of his mind when, middle of the day, in our tiny alley, he pointed his gun to the third floor where the police uncle lived and fired four times.
It was difficult to get to sleep; our bodies now jumped at the slightest noise
‘Motherfucker, wait,’ said the shaking retired cop from his balcony. ‘Motherfucker, you just wait, I’m gon get you fucked up.’
All this was relayed to me via WhatsApp by my best friend, who was watching it unfold. ‘Maybe don’t come home tonight,’ she texted me.

By that night, the boy had fled the scene, and police uncle was having it out in the alley with the boy’s wife. A chair was hurled, unclear who hurled it upon whom, and a few nights later, men with guns were at our door. When the story was pieced together over the following days, it was already too late: fear had lodged itself in our bodies; we now jumped at the slightest noise.
‘No one will enter your house just like that,’ the grocery store uncle said.
‘But if they come back…?’ I asked him.
‘That ice-boy needs to go,’ he said. ‘If nowhere else then to rehab.’
‘But his wife is pregnant,’ I said, and realised how deep I was in Badar Commercial gossip and lore.

Something I learned living alone-together in Badar Commercial, and that I want younger women to know, is that we are actually never guaranteed safety. Therefore, one way to collect the guts and energy to move out of your parents’ home and make a life alone in this city is to realise that the question is not whether we are safe but what the cost is, the violent cost, of trying to live a full life in this city and world.

At Badar, the cost for me was estrangement from my relatives, especially my aunts whom I loved but who knew nothing about my feminist life anymore. The other cost was a new edginess – always alert for the 3 am bang on the door. Then there were the men who tailed me while I cycled, who lurked outside our building, the officer who showed up with my full name at my door, who wanted me to know he knew I lived here.

Still, none of the fear these men instilled in us came close to the body-wreckage from the violence and betrayal we had known inside our own homes. Under our family’s so-called protection, we were surveilled and shamed in the same breath. Men, assigned as our guardians and teachers, hurt us. In my case, it was my cousin and my music teacher. The worst part was having to continue showing them respect. That kind of lying festers inside the body, when everyone knows that danger for women is two feet away, at home. It’s a trap to think we have ever overcome danger. As a result, I have spent my life watching men’s gazes for that livewire glint. The ones on the street I can usually recognise and quickly counter. The home gaze is tricker because I cannot anticipate when and where it might suddenly appear.

As the streets got to know me and I them, some knots in my body loosened, knots that had to do with the entanglement of class and gender politics, of who is portrayed as a threat versus where the actual danger lies. Other un-knottings had to do with feeling free in practice, not just theory, cycling around Badar in shorts and shalwar kameez.
I told my aunts the truth about my life. What was the point of all this public and street freedom if nothing changed in the hardest of spaces: at home?

As the knots loosened, other cities opened within us. A parent’s death; a friend’s secret abortion; walking away from a marriage; walking towards ourselves. We learned that it is possible to live within four walls that hold our grief, not just cause it – that can take it all, and more and more and more. I’d spent my 20s chasing freedom in the streets because I’d never imagined an inner space – the apartment, my room, but really, a space within – that could feel like home, where you don’t feel trapped or sealed or estranged. This indoor city opens up what you can do with your body in the cities outside, so that one day, in that same Badar Commercial, I chased a man away with a chappal because he was following me. I chased him away, wielding that slipper with a confidence that came from having lived in Badar for three years now. How familiar the streets felt; how I knew that they would not betray me.
Another time, however, I ran home breathless and called M J for help, worried I had been followed home. Limits of bravery differ day by day.
‘I’m coming to pick you up,’ he said. ‘Let’s get you some air by the sea.’
